title: The body's matter
hook: the senses, the body's life, its heat, its nourishment

segments.voice: Yesterday, rupa, matter, and the four that head its list: hardness, cohesion, heat and motion. Your line: four great elements.

What's the difference between your hand and the table it's resting on? By yesterday's account, both are made of the same four great elements. Both are hard, both hold together, both have a temperature, both press. Yet one of them can feel the other, and the other can't. One gets warm from the inside, gets hungry, heals a cut. The table does none of that. So the manual keeps going past the four, into the kinds of matter that belong only to a living body.
screen: `YOUR HAND, AND THE TABLE.` → `THE SAME FOUR ELEMENTS.` → `ONE OF THEM FEELS.`

segments.voice: Start with the senses. In the Abhidhamma, the eye that sees isn't the eyeball. It's a fine, sensitive matter inside it, ready to be struck by color. The same sensitive matter sits in the ear, the nose, the tongue and the whole surface of the body: five doors where the world gets in. A table has none. Next, life. The manual names a kind of matter called the life faculty, which keeps the other living matter going, the way a caretaker keeps a garden watered. When it stops, the four great elements are still there, but the body is no longer alive. Then heat. Here temperature is one of the forces that keeps producing matter, moment after moment: warmth in a living body is part of what keeps it being made. And nourishment. Food, in this system, carries a subtle nutritive essence, and that essence keeps producing matter too. So the manual names four things that keep matter arising: past kamma, the mind, temperature and food. A table gets only one. A living body gets all four. Notice what the list never adds: a fifth thing, a soul or a self. A living body is matter held up by more conditions, not matter with someone hiding inside. In one sutta the Buddha says the world, its arising and its ending are found in this fathom-long body, with its perception and mind. The Abhidhamma takes him at his word and starts measuring.
screen: `FIVE SENSITIVE DOORS.` · `THE LIFE FACULTY KEEPS IT GOING.` · `HEAT AND FOOD KEEP MAKING MATTER.` · then, large: `NO ONE HIDING INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Bring your attention to your hands and notice their warmth, without deciding whether it's pleasant. Then let attention move to the belly, the chest, the back of the neck, and rest wherever there's warmth: the body doing its work, moment by moment, without your help. If you like, place one palm over the other and feel heat meeting heat.
The body's matter. The sense doors, the life faculty, and the heat and food that keep a living body being made. Today's word.
Your line: living matter. A hand and a table share the same four elements, and only one of them can feel. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn the kinds of matter found only in living bodies, such as the sense organs' sensitive matter and the life faculty, and some meditation teachers in the Theravada tradition guide students to feel warmth and other qualities in the body directly.

chat.says: If a hand and a table are both just matter, what makes the hand alive?
options: The manual names sense doors, a life faculty, and heat and food that keep making it.
A hidden self lives inside the hand, and the table simply doesn't have one.
The hand has more of the four elements packed into it than the table.
chat.meaning: The Abhidhamma adds kinds of matter only living bodies have, kept arising by kamma, mind, heat and food. It never adds a soul or self.

Abhidhamma.meaning: the higher teaching, the third basket of the Pali canon

life faculty.meaning: the matter that keeps a body's other living matter going

kamma.meaning: action; here, past action, one of four things that produce matter

sutta.meaning: a discourse of the Buddha, kept in the Pali canon

notes: Five sensitive kinds of matter (pasada rupa) and the life faculty (jivitindriya) as listed in Abhidhammattha Sangaha VI; confirm.
The caretaker/garden simile for the life faculty is the writer's own image; the Visuddhimagga's simile (water maintaining lotuses, or a ferryman) may be preferred by a Keeper.
'Heat' here is temperature (utu) as one of the four producers of matter; the index's 'its heat' might also be read as the digestive fire. Confirm framing.
Four origins of matter (kamma, citta, utu, ahara) per Sangaha VI; 'a table gets only one' (temperature-born matter) is the standard reading for external matter; confirm.
AN 4.45 (Rohitassa) is paraphrased; confirm the reference and wording.
Original: Devanagari spelling of jivitindriya; confirm.
